newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar seen staying firm in the near term.
newsitem.headline: Dollar seen staying firm in the near term.

text.p: The dollar will likely stay firm against the yen towards the end of March, but a downside risk remains in the long-term, according to a Reuters poll of leading economists released on Thursday.
The forecasts from 27 private economists in Tokyo and London showed that on average they expected the dollar at 115.16 yen by the end of March.
But the economists added that little change was expected in the overall bullish sentiment for the greenback in the near term.
The survey was conducted between January 13 and 16, but since then the dollar has jumped further and was above the 119 yen level on Thursday.
Since the beginning of 1997, the dollar has been rising against major currencies, including the yen and the mark, as a result of gains in U.S. stocks and a vigorous U.S. economy.
"We have been looking for the yen to depreciate and we still think that depreciation has further to go," said Michael Hartnett, chief economist at Merrill Lynch in Tokyo.
The survey covered 37 brokerages and research bodies, although not all those polled responded to all the questions.
Mamoru Yamazaki, senior economist at Paribas Capital Markets Limited, agreed. "I think the sentiment for the yen will remain bearish for a while," he said.
Yamazaki said his initial forecast of 113 yen for the end of March should be revised to 118 yen because of the recent strong movements of the dollar.
Strong buying interest in foreign assets from Japanese operators, as well as the fragility of Tokyo share prices will also encourage further yen sales against the dollar, he said.
On Tuesday, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan underpinned the bullish dollar sentiment by delivering an upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy to the Senate Budget Committee.
Greenspan said U.S. labour markets were "exceptionally tight" but that that had not led to accelerated wages or inflation.
The dollar's advance against the yen has also been supported by weakness of the mark and other currencies.
Uncertainty over Europe's Economic Monetary Union (EMU) and weak German economic data released in the past few weeks were behind such movements, analysts said.
But many economists expected the dollar to fall gradually against the yen in the longer-term.

"The dollar is likely to be dragged down on speculation that U.S. interest rates will be raised at the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in March," said Hideki Naito, a managing analyst at MMS in Tokyo.

He said a rise in U.S. interest rates would prompt sales of U.S. Treasuries, which could weaken the dollar against the yen, and for this reason forecast that the dollar would fall to 112 yen by the end of March.
The possible liquidation of foreign securities to help offset losses in domestic stocks by Japanese institutional investors may be another factor to weaken the dollar.
"Japanese operators might start to sell off their foreign assets to cover losses before the book-closing in March, which would support the yen," said Naito.
The highest forecast for the end of March was 120 yen and the lowest 107.50 yen.
Average forecasts in the poll showed the dollar at 114.40 yen at the end of June, 111.99 yen at the end of September and 109.94 yen at the end of December.
